newsitem.title: USA: Doctor tells of amputation on Oklahoma bomb victim.
newsitem.headline: Doctor tells of amputation on Oklahoma bomb victim.

text.p: A surgeon on Thursday described in chilling detail how he amputated the leg of a woman trapped in the rubble after the April 1995 Oklahoma City bombing.

As the government pushed for the death penalty for convicted bomber Timothy McVeigh, Dr. James Sullivan, who rushed to the bombed-out Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, said he crawled on his belly through the rubble to reach Daina Bradley, who was trapped in a crevice.

At one point, the orthopedic surgeon said, he mistakenly thought the amputation was over only to find the leg was still connected. "She was still attached and she screamed," he said, explaining that he was trying to perform the surgery quickly because of the instability of the collapsed building.
Eventually he completed the operation and the woman, who lost her mother and her two children in the bombing, survived.

Since Wednesday prosecutors have been presenting emotional evidence from survivors, people who lost loved ones and rescue workers sent to the Murrah building, where 168 people died. The prosecution was trying to persuade a jury of seven men and five women to call for the death penalty for McVeigh, who was found guilty on Monday of blowing up the office building.

The jury was hearing evidence in the penalty phase of the trial to determine if McVeigh, 29, should be put to death or spend the rest of his life in prison. On Wednesday 15 people took the stand to tell how their lives will never be the same.

In a reversal, federal Judge Richard Matsch did not allow 9-year-old Clint Seidl, whose mother died in the blast, to testify. "I believe it would be inflammatory for him to testify, a boy of that age and obvious innocence," he said.

Testimony on Thursday was again heart-wrenching with several witnesses bursting into tears and one breaking down on the stand. McVeigh, who has sat expressionless throughout the trial, blinked rapidly during testimony by a man who lost his father, as if affected by what he was hearing.

The right-handed physician told the court that because the area where Bradley was trapped was so small he had to crawl to her and perform the amputation with his left hand. He said he could not give her any anaesthesia because she was in shock and having difficulty breathing in the dusty atmosphere.

He did give her a drug that would make her forget the operation and while he was waiting for it to take effect he prayed. "I prayed she wouldn't die as a result of my treatment and if I died, my family would remember me," he said.

Ruth Hightower, 60, whose daughter died in a nearby building, had to fight back tears from the moment she got on the stand. She is now caring for her daugher's two children, both of whom have been emotionally affected, she said.

Prosecutors were expected to wrap up their part in the penalty phase sometime on Thursday. The defence will make an opening statement, probably on Friday, and call its own witnesses to try to persuade the jury to spare McVeigh's life and opt instead for life in prison without parole.
